evidence: Cic. N. D. 2.140: Sēnsūs autem interpretēs ac nūntiī rērum
Cic. de Or. 3.99: gustātus, quī est sēnsus ex omnibus maximē voluptārius
terms.comment: The five are vīsus (sight), audītus (hearing), odōrātus (smell), gustātus (taste) and tāctus (touch) (Traupman 58–59).

phrases.latin: cum autem paulum firmitātis accessit, et animō ūtuntur et sēnsibus cōnītunturque, ut sēsē ērigant, et manibus ūtuntur et eōs agnōscunt, ā quibus ēducantur
phrases.english: but when they have a little strength, they use their minds and their senses, try to stand up, use their hands, and know the people who are bringing them up

phrases.latin: Sēnsūs autem interpretēs ac nūntiī rērum in capite tamquam in arce mīrificē ad ūsūs necessāriōs et factī et conlocātī sunt.
phrases.english: The senses, the interpreters and messengers of things, have been made and placed in the head, as in a citadel, wonderfully fitted for what we need.

sources: Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-cicero-philosophica), as checked there against the editions they name.
Cic. de Or. 3.99 and N. D. 2.140 checked against the Perseus Latin texts (9 November 2026).
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 58–59.
